title: The Real Villain in Your Tech Stack: How to Tame Legacy Systems
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni frames legacy systems as a villain that slows innovation and argues that empathy is the tool for taming them. She tells three workplace stories: dashboards built on a legacy tool that did not scale, a customer service team that kept using a classic CRM interface and created duplicate records, and a Six Sigma colleague whose process-improvement project stalled because stakeholders feared for their jobs. In each, the solution is leader-oriented rather than technical: show leadership the cost, train on the modern system and bring team leaders along, and hold the hard conversations up front with an executive preface. The Doctor Who framing is decoration, but the change-management lesson that people resist what threatens their identity is useful and plainly stated.
points: Legacy tools carry hidden maintenance and opportunity costs that are best made visible to leadership.
Duplicate records in the CRM case were traced to a usability problem on the customer service side, not carelessness.
Training only on the modern system, showing users the benefit and bringing their leaders along helped adoption.
Resistance to process change often comes from people protecting their role and identity, so the purpose should be explained by an executive sponsor early.
Listening for pain points and negotiating for mutual wins is the practical influence method.
quotes: Villains slow you down and interrupt your progress. The villain of legacy tech has the potential to do the same.
This worked great in the first few weeks. In the coming months, however, it began to sabotage our scalability.

I demonstrated to leadership the time it took to maintain and offer options to upgrade the visual displays to a newer system. I collaborated with other folks in our data team to tackle how we could best consolidate.

On average, 31% of an organization's tech is made up of Legacy systems. Yuck. Even worse, it drains opportunity cost, meaning time could be spent elsewhere on more productive measures rather than maintaining the status quo.

The reason was revealed after some Q&A sessions—they could not find the source of the truth record, so they just created a new one. This was an overcomplication of something that should have been simple - finding the existing record.

With moving away from legacy systems and processes, tough conversations sometimes must be had. Tackle them with empathy, compassion, and open ears. It is better to have these conversations up front vs. avoid them.
If you want change, you must influence decision-makers and detractors. Empathy is a component of strong emotional intelligence, and it will be your strongest tool for making progress.
